items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Rather than + -ing), mid-sentence blank before a colon; the plant is the right subject
items.passage: Rather than exposing their entire leaves to the intense southern African sun, ______ only the translucent tips stay visible, channeling light to the underground tissue.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the leaves of the pebble-like succulents called lithops are kept mostly buried in the soil:
there is soil covering most of each leaf of the pebble-like succulents called lithops:
the pebble-like succulents called lithops keep most of each leaf buried in the soil:
most of each leaf of the pebble-like succulents called lithops is kept buried in the soil:
items.explanation: Only a plant can avoid exposing its own leaves, so the noun right after the opening phrase must name the plants. Choice C places “the pebble-like succulents called lithops” there, so the sentence clearly says that these plants, rather than exposing their whole leaves, keep most of each leaf buried.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the plant’s leaves, in a “the Y of X” phrase
A.why_wrong: The head of the subject is “the leaves,” so the sentence illogically says that the leaves avoid exposing their own entire leaves.

B.recipe: expletive opener (E), built on a different noun
B.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving “Rather than exposing their entire leaves” without a noun it can logically describe.

D.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
D.why_wrong: “Most of each leaf” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that part of a leaf avoids exposing the plant’s entire leaves.

items.notes: Subject: lithops leaf windows (science, botany). Band-7 setting from 37e5c794: one-sentence passage, mid-sentence blank, options end in a colon, 12 words of the run after the blank; the plants are named only inside the options, so every option carries the same long phrase (as in 2bca654a) and the closest distractors (A, D) keep every fact with the leaves as subject. The expletive (B) is built on “soil,” not on the key’s subject. Recipes W, E, V. Options 14 to 16 words, key the shortest.

band7.why: Plain-thing key on the shape of the one band-7 prep_gerund official (37e5c794): A keeps every fact with “the leaves of ... lithops” as subject, where “their” can be misread as pointing inside the subject; D is a passive on part of a leaf, B an expletive built on another noun. Every option is a grammatical clause ending in a colon; the only fault is what the opener describes. Weakest point: the cue sits in the opener, not downstream.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Estimated at), passage-final blank; the right subject is a property (the plant’s growth rate), not the plant
items.passage: The yareta, a cushion plant native to the high Andes, resembles a mossy boulder but actually consists of thousands of tightly clustered stems. Estimated at roughly 1.5 centimeters annually, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the yareta’s growth rate is so slow that its largest cushions are thought to be thousands of years old.
the yareta grows so slowly that its largest cushions are thought to be thousands of years old.
the yareta’s cushions grow so slowly that the largest ones are thought to be thousands of years old.
it is thought that the yareta’s largest cushions, given how slowly the plant grows, are thousands of years old.
items.explanation: What can be estimated at about 1.5 centimeters per year is a rate of growth, not a plant. Choice A places “the yareta’s growth rate” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the growth rate.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun keeps every fact
B.why_wrong: “The yareta” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the plant itself is estimated at 1.5 centimeters per year.

C.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W), built on the obvious noun in a possessive
C.why_wrong: The head of “the yareta’s cushions” is “cushions,” so the sentence says that the cushions, not their rate of growth, are estimated at 1.5 centimeters per year.

D.recipe: expletive opener (E), built on “it is thought,” not on the key’s subject
D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: yareta (Azorella compacta), Andean cushion plant (science, botany). Band-7 setting from 2dd1b8bf and fced396a: the opener describes a property, so the right subject is a noun phrase built on the obvious noun (“the yareta’s growth rate”); B keeps every fact with the plant as subject, C opens with the same possessive as the key. Recipes W, W (possessive head), E. Options 17 to 19 words; key not the longest.

band7.why: Property key as in fced396a and 2dd1b8bf: only a rate can be “estimated at 1.5 centimeters annually,” while B keeps every fact with the obvious noun (the plant) and C opens with the same possessive as the key. Options run 17 to 19 words (doc range 12 to 16), but the key is not the longest, so length gives nothing away.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener, passage-final blank; the animal is the right subject
items.passage: The aye-aye, a nocturnal lemur endemic to Madagascar, feeds primarily on wood-boring beetle larvae concealed inside living trees. Tapping rapidly on bark with its elongated, skeletal middle finger, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the hollow sound of a tunnel tells the aye-aye where to gnaw through the wood to reach a larva.
the aye-aye listens for the hollow sound of a tunnel and then gnaws through the wood to reach a larva.
the aye-aye’s large ears pick up the hollow sound of a tunnel, revealing where to gnaw through the wood.
a tunnel’s hollow sound is detected by the aye-aye, which then gnaws through the wood to reach a larva.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes an animal tapping on bark with its finger. Choice B places “the aye-aye” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the aye-aye does the tapping.

A.why_wrong: “The hollow sound of a tunnel” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the sound taps on bark with a finger.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the aye-aye’s large ears,” so the sentence illogically says that the ears tap on bark with a finger.

D.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
D.why_wrong: “A tunnel’s hollow sound” follows the phrase, so the sentence says that the sound does the tapping.

items.notes: Subject: aye-aye percussive foraging (science, zoology). Band 6: plain agent key as in 3.14 and 3.5, three recipes W, P, V; no expletive, so no option wraps the key in “it is ... that”; options 19 to 20 words, key not the longest. “Its” in the opener points forward to the subject, as “their” does in the official items.

band7.why: Plain agent key (the aye-aye) with W, P and V distractors, the band-6 shape of 9df6da04 and dab8b8ee; no expletive, so nothing wraps the key in “it is ... that”; band_target 6 as planned.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural possessive determiner before a singular head, relative clause with a plural noun between head and verb
items.passage: More than a thousand years ago, Hohokam farmers dug hundreds of kilometers of irrigation canals across what is now central Arizona. Their canal network, whose principal channels diverted water from the Salt and Gila Rivers, ______ among the most extensive irrigation systems built anywhere in the ancient Americas.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “network,” so it needs the singular verb “remains.” The plural words around it (“Their,” “channels,” “Rivers”) do not change the subject’s number.

A.why_wrong: “Remain” is plural and agrees with the nearby plural “Rivers” or “channels,” not with the singular subject “network.”

B.why_wrong: “Are remaining” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “network.”

C.why_wrong: “Have remained” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “network.”

items.notes: Subject: Hohokam canals, Arizona (history, archaeology). Band 6: plural possessor “Their” before the singular head, then a “whose” clause with a plural noun and a number-neutral verb (“diverted”), and the plural “Rivers” right before the blank, opposite to the key. Head to blank 13 words. All distractors plural in three tenses, as the bank does.

fixes: notes only: whose-clause verb named as “drew”; the passage has “diverted”

band7.why: Plural determiner “Their” before the singular head, then a whose-clause with two plural attractors (channels, Rivers) and the number-neutral “diverted”; 13 words head to blank, all three distractors plural. No intervener verb of the other number, so a strong band 6 as planned.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener, mid-sentence blank before the main verb; the work, not its author, is the right subject
items.passage: A lyrical portrait of western Hunan, the mountainous region of rivers and market towns where Chinese novelist Shen Congwen spent his childhood, ______ follows Cuicui, a ferryman’s granddaughter, as she comes of age.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Shen wrote the novella Border Town (1934), which, set in a river town near the Sichuan border,
the setting of Shen’s novella Border Town (1934), a river town near the Sichuan border,
Shen’s novella Border Town (1934), set in a river town near the Sichuan border,
set in a river town near the Sichuan border, Shen wrote the novella Border Town (1934), which
items.explanation: A lyrical portrait of a region is a work of writing, so the noun right after the opening phrase must name the work. Choice C places “Shen’s novella Border Town (1934)” there, so the phrase correctly describes the novella, and the verb “follows” then tells what the novella does.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the author, with the work moved into a relative clause
A.why_wrong: “Shen” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the writer himself is a lyrical portrait of the region.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the setting
B.why_wrong: “The setting” of the novella follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the setting is a portrait of the region and that the setting follows Cuicui.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W) after a second, misplaced modifier
D.why_wrong: After two modifiers, “Shen” is the subject, so the sentence says that Shen is both a portrait of the region and set in a river town.

items.notes: Subject: Shen Congwen’s Border Town (literature). The plan set band 7, but R3_appositive has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md), so this is written as a strong band 6 on the shape of 3.7 (5b8f9cf2): mid-sentence blank, options are fragments that join the main verb “follows,” and all four share the same facts. Key is the shortest option, as in 3.7; B also ends in a comma, so the key is not the only option without “which.” One-sentence passage (33 words).

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md appendix), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 on 5b8f9cf2 (3.7): fragment options joining the main verb “follows,” two of them with Shen as subject and one with the setting.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: individual possession by two plural possessors, cue after the blank
items.passage: Golden moles, which inhabit southern Africa, and marsupial moles, which inhabit Australian deserts, last shared a common ancestor more than 100 million years ago. Yet ______ bodies have converged on remarkably similar adaptations for burrowing: in each group, tiny vestigial eyes lie concealed beneath skin and fur, and enlarged foreclaws allow the animal to “swim” through loose sand.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The bodies belong to two separate groups of animals, each with its own bodies (“in each group”), so each plural noun needs its own plural possessive apostrophe: “golden moles’ and marsupial moles’.”

A.why_wrong: “Golden moles” and “marsupial moles” are plain plurals here; the context requires the plural possessives “golden moles’” and “marsupial moles’.”

C.recipe: missing apostrophe plus wrong possessor number
C.why_wrong: The context requires the plural possessive “golden moles’,” not the plain plural, and the plural possessive “marsupial moles’,” not the singular “marsupial mole’s.”

D.recipe: joint possession where each group has its own (individual possession)
D.why_wrong: Putting the apostrophe only on the second noun suggests a single set of bodies shared by both groups, but the text describes each group’s bodies separately.

items.notes: Subject: golden moles and marsupial moles, convergent evolution (science, zoology). Band-7 setting: individual possession as in 4c335aea, here with generic plural possessors as in 2784cbaf (objects’); the deciding cue (“in each group”) comes 13 words after the blank. Option set mirrors 4c335aea (both plain, plain plus wrong possessive, joint). The bare plural (A) is offered and is wrong because a plural noun cannot modify another noun here (“marsupial moles bodies”); no singular attributive form (“marsupial mole bodies”) is offered, since that would be acceptable. Key is the longest by one or two characters, as in 4c335aea.

band7.why: Individual possession with generic plural possessors, option set slot for slot as 4c335aea, cue (“in each group”) 13 words after the blank. D (joint possession) fails for CB’s 4c335aea reason: bodies cannot belong to both groups together, and “have converged” plus “in each group” need two separate sets. No attributive singular (“marsupial mole bodies”) is offered, so no second defensible option.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: absolute phrase (possessive noun + past participle) after a complete clause; finite options make comma splices
items.passage: Constructed in the 1350s under the Marinid sultan Abu Inan Faris, the Bou Inania Madrasa in Fez, Morocco, is celebrated for its intricate ornamentation, its courtyard walls ______ in geometric zellige tilework beneath friezes of carved stucco and cedar.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence is already complete after “ornamentation,” so what follows the comma must be a supplement, not a second main clause. The past participle “sheathed” forms the phrase “its courtyard walls sheathed in ... tilework,” which describes the madrasa’s decoration.

A.why_wrong: “Are sheathed” makes “its courtyard walls are sheathed ...” a second main clause joined to the first with only a comma.

B.why_wrong: “Have been sheathed” creates a second main clause joined to the first with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: “Were sheathed” creates a second main clause joined to the first with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: Bou Inania Madrasa, Fez (arts, architecture). Band-7 setting from c88ba1b7 and 81f09e07: a possessive noun before the blank lets every finite option form a full clause, so each distractor is a comma splice, not a fragment; “are sheathed” also matches the present “is celebrated.” “Sheathed in” has no object slot, so the key cannot be read as a finite past verb.

band7.why: Absolute phrase after a complete clause, a close mirror of c88ba1b7 (“is remembered for its grandeur ..., its vehicles ______”): the noun before the blank lets every finite option form a full clause, so each distractor is a comma splice, and “are sheathed” also matches the present “is celebrated.” “Sheathed in” has no object slot, so the key cannot read as finite.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head with a participial phrase of singular nouns before the blank
items.passage: Kalamkari, a textile tradition of southern India, takes its name from the kalam, a bamboo pen saturated with vegetable dyes. In Srikalahasti, artisans drawing freehand with this pen on a single cotton panel ______ elaborate episodes from Hindu epics such as the Ramayana.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the plural noun “artisans,” so it needs the plural verb “depict.” The phrase “drawing freehand with this pen on a single cotton panel” only describes the artisans.

B.why_wrong: “Depicts” is singular and agrees with “panel” or “pen,” not with the plural subject “artisans.”

C.why_wrong: “Is depicting” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “artisans.”

D.why_wrong: “Has depicted” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “artisans.”

items.notes: Subject: kalamkari, Srikalahasti (arts, textiles). Medium: plural head behind a 10-word participial phrase holding two singular nouns, the singular “panel” right before the blank.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: plural object pronoun with singular rival nouns nearby
items.passage: The cookie-cutter shark’s underside glows with photophores except for a dark collar across its throat, which, seen from below, may resemble a small fish. Predators attracted to this decoy rarely get a meal; instead, the shark latches onto ______ with its lips and twists, carving out a circular plug of flesh.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The shark latches onto the predators that were attracted to the decoy. “Predators” is plural, so the plural pronoun “them” is needed.

A.why_wrong: “It” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “predators.”

B.why_wrong: “This” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “predators.”

C.why_wrong: “That” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “predators.”

items.notes: Subject: cookie-cutter shark (science, marine biology). Medium: singular rival nouns (collar, fish, decoy, meal, shark) sit between the antecedent and the pronoun; “one” is not offered because “one” of the predators would be acceptable.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid (possessor + possessed noun), number cue “each”
items.passage: Brazilian novelist Graciliano Ramos’s Vidas Secas (Barren Lives), published in 1938, follows a family fleeing drought in the backlands of northeastern Brazil. Though the family members rarely speak, the novel conveys each ______ through a narrator who moves freely between their minds, even entering that of their dog.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Each” calls for a singular noun, and the thoughts belong to that character, so the singular possessive “character’s” is needed; “thoughts” is a plain plural, so it takes no apostrophe.

A.why_wrong: “Characters” is a plain plural, but the context requires the singular possessive “character’s.”

C.why_wrong: “Characters’” is a plural possessive, but “each” requires the singular “character’s.”

D.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
D.why_wrong: “Thought’s” is possessive, but nothing belongs to the thoughts; the plain plural “thoughts” is needed.

items.notes: Subject: Graciliano Ramos, Vidas Secas (literature). Medium: partial grid as in 2.24, with the number cue “each” right before the blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: compound subject whose two parts each carry a participial phrase with singular nouns
items.passage: Papiamento, predominantly spoken on the Caribbean islands of Aruba, Bonaire, and Curaçao, and Chavacano, concentrated in and around the Philippine city of Zamboanga, ______ both creole languages whose vocabularies derive largely from Spanish or Portuguese.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is compound: “Papiamento ... and Chavacano.” Two subjects joined by “and” take the plural verb “are.”

A.why_wrong: “Is” is singular and agrees with the nearby “Zamboanga,” not with the compound subject.

B.why_wrong: “Was” is singular and doesn’t agree with the compound subject.

D.why_wrong: “Has been” is singular and doesn’t agree with the compound subject.

items.notes: Subject: Papiamento and Chavacano (social science, linguistics). Medium: the conjunction sits 12 words into the subject, after a list of singular island names, and the singular “Zamboanga” comes right before the blank. Frame differs from 2.13 (each conjunct carries its own participle).

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner their vs its and contractions, antecedent 12 words back with singular nouns between
items.passage: The Minangkabau people of West Sumatra, Indonesia, form one of the world’s largest matrilineal societies. Traditional Minangkabau longhouses, constructed of timber and elevated on stilts above the ground, are known for ______ upswept roof peaks, whose curving silhouettes resemble a water buffalo’s horns.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The roof peaks belong to the longhouses, a plural noun, so the plural possessive determiner “their” is needed.

B.why_wrong: “Its” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “longhouses.”

C.why_wrong: “They’re” means “they are,” which doesn’t make sense before “upswept roof peaks.”

D.why_wrong: “It’s” means “it is” and is singular, so it fits neither the meaning nor the antecedent.

items.notes: Subject: Minangkabau longhouses (social science, anthropology). Medium: antecedent 12 words before the blank, with the singular “timber” and “ground” in between; no singular noun before the blank could own roof peaks.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: main verb after a subordinate clause
items.passage: When a thunderstorm’s cold downdraft strikes dry desert ground, the outflowing air ______ loose dust and sand into a towering, rapidly advancing wall known in Sudan as a haboob.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause has the subject “the outflowing air” but no main verb. The finite verb “lifts” supplies it.

A.why_wrong: The participle “lifting” doesn’t give the main clause a finite verb.

C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to lift” doesn’t give the main clause a finite verb.

D.why_wrong: “Having lifted” doesn’t give the main clause a finite verb.

items.notes: Subject: haboobs (science, meteorology). Canonical easy option set; the “When” clause has its own verb, so the student must see that the main clause still lacks one.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: main verb after a plural subject
items.passage: Ogham, an early Irish alphabet, consists of strokes and notches carved along the edges of stones. Most surviving ogham inscriptions ______ little more than an individual’s name and an ancestor’s name.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence has the subject “Most surviving ogham inscriptions” but no main verb. The finite verb “record” supplies it.

A.why_wrong: The participle “recording” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to record” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

C.why_wrong: “Having recorded” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: ogham inscriptions (social science, writing systems). Canonical easy option set; two-sentence shape as 1.21 and 1.30.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: singular subject pronoun for a named person
items.passage: In 1613, samurai Hasekura Tsunenaga left Japan as an ambassador of the feudal lord Date Masamune, crossing the Pacific to Mexico and then the Atlantic to Spain. In 1615, ______ reached Rome, the farthest destination of a diplomatic mission that would last seven years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The person who traveled and reached Rome is Hasekura Tsunenaga, one man, so the singular pronoun “he” is needed.

B.why_wrong: “They” is plural, but only one traveler, Hasekura, is named as making the journey.

C.why_wrong: “It” refers to a thing, not to a person such as Hasekura.

D.why_wrong: “Those” is plural and has no plural antecedent in the text.

items.notes: Subject: Hasekura Tsunenaga’s embassy (history). Easy: the antecedent is the subject of the previous sentence; no rival person travels.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head with a short participial interrupter
items.passage: American astronomer Daniel Kirkwood noticed several nearly empty bands in the asteroid belt. These gaps, named after him, ______ caused by gravitational resonances with Jupiter.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the plural noun “gaps,” so it needs the plural verb “are.” The phrase “named after him” only describes the gaps.

A.why_wrong: “Is” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “gaps.”

B.why_wrong: “Was” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “gaps.”

D.why_wrong: “Has been” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “gaps.”

items.notes: Subject: Kirkwood gaps (science, astronomy). Easy: subject behind a three-word interrupter with no number clash.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head, no intervener
items.passage: Mongolia’s morin khuur, or horsehead fiddle, has two strings traditionally made of horsehair. The instrument ______ named for the carved horse’s head that tops its neck.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “instrument,” so it needs the singular verb “is.”

A.why_wrong: “Are” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “instrument.”

C.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “instrument.”

D.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “instrument”; it may attract a student who looks back at “two strings.”

items.notes: Subject: morin khuur (arts, music). Easy: subject right before the blank; the plural “two strings” in the first sentence is the only attractor.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular pronoun subject, no intervener
items.passage: Iranian writer Sadegh Hedayat’s novel The Blind Owl is narrated by a reclusive painter of lacquered pen cases. On every case, he ______ an identical scene: an old man beneath a cypress and a woman offering a flower.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “he” is singular, so it needs the singular verb “paints.”

A.why_wrong: “Paint” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “he.”

B.why_wrong: “Are painting” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “he.”

C.why_wrong: “Have painted” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “he.”

items.notes: Subject: Sadegh Hedayat’s The Blind Owl (literature). Easy: pronoun subject right before the blank, as in 1.6.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a habitual action, with present verbs throughout
items.passage: Honeypot ants live in arid regions of North America and Australia, where food is frequently scarce. Specialized workers called repletes are fed nectar by their nestmates until their abdomens become enormously distended. During droughts, the repletes ______ this stored food with the rest of the colony.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes what honeypot ants regularly do, using present-tense verbs (“live,” “are fed,” “become”). The simple present “share” fits this repeated, ongoing behavior.

A.recipe: simple past where the present is needed
A.why_wrong: “Shared” places a habitual behavior in the past, which doesn’t match the present-tense description.

B.why_wrong: “Were sharing” describes an ongoing action in the past, not a habit that continues today.

D.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
D.why_wrong: “Had shared” places the action before another past time, but the text describes a present habit.

items.notes: Subject: honeypot ant repletes (science, entomology). Easy: habitual cue “During droughts” plus present verbs in both earlier sentences.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: full 2 x 2 grid (singular possessor + plural noun)
items.passage: American composer Louis Hardin, known as Moondog, spent years performing on a Manhattan street corner in a homemade Viking helmet and cloak, playing percussion instruments of his own invention. Many of the ______ are rounds and canons, compositions in which a melody is repeated by successively entering voices.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pieces belong to one composer, Moondog, so the singular possessive “composer’s” is needed; “pieces” is a plain plural with nothing belonging to it, so it takes no apostrophe.

B.why_wrong: “Composers” is a plain plural, but the pieces belong to one composer, so the singular possessive “composer’s” is needed.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Piece’s” is possessive, but nothing belongs to the pieces; the plain plural “pieces” is needed.

D.why_wrong: This choice drops the apostrophe the possessor needs and adds one to “pieces,” which needs none.

items.notes: Subject: Moondog (arts, music). Easy: full 2 x 2 grid as in 1.16, cue the single named composer.

fixes: dropped the label “Blind” before “American composer Louis Hardin” (house style; not needed by the item); word_count 49 to 48

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor + plural noun after “each of the”
items.passage: The four-eyed fish (Anableps anableps), which inhabits brackish estuaries of northern South America, actually possesses only two eyes. However, a horizontal band of tissue divides each of the ______ into separate upper and lower halves, enabling the fish to see above and below the waterline simultaneously.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The eyes belong to one animal, the four-eyed fish, so the singular possessive “animal’s” is needed. “Each of the” calls for a plural noun, and nothing belongs to the eyes, so “eyes” is a plain plural.

A.why_wrong: “Animals” is a plain plural, but the eyes belong to one animal, so the possessive “animal’s” is needed.

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Eye’s” is a singular possessive, but after “each of the” the plain plural “eyes” is needed.

C.recipe: wrong possessor number and needless apostrophe
C.why_wrong: “Animals’” is plural, but the text describes one fish, and “eye’s” wrongly makes the eyes possessive.

items.notes: Subject: four-eyed fish (science, zoology). Easy: the singular possessor is cued by “The four-eyed fish ... possesses.”

fixes: notes only: cue quoted as “has”; the passage says “possesses”

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: to-infinitive of purpose after a complete clause
items.passage: In 1994, middle school students in Kaktovik, Alaska, developed a system of written numerals ______ the base-20 counting structure of the Iñupiaq language, which conventional decimal digits could not easily express.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “students ... developed a system of written numerals” is already complete, so the blank must begin a phrase, not a second main verb. The infinitive “to represent” explains the purpose of the numerals.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
A.why_wrong: “Represented” makes a second main verb with no conjunction to join it to “developed.”

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
C.why_wrong: “Represents” makes a second main verb with no conjunction to join it to “developed.”

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
D.why_wrong: “Is representing” makes a second main verb with no conjunction to join it to “developed.”

items.notes: Subject: Kaktovik numerals (social science, mathematics and language). Easy: purpose infinitive after a complete clause, as 1.22.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate
items.passage: In 1948, physician Geoffrey Orbell led a small search party into the remote, rugged Murchison Mountains of New Zealand’s Fiordland region and ______ a living population of takahē, large flightless birds that most scientists had presumed extinct for half a century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “And” joins a second verb to the first verb, “led,” so the blank needs a finite past-tense verb like “led.” “Found” completes the compound predicate “led ... and found.”

A.why_wrong: “Finding” doesn’t match the finite verb “led” that “and” connects it to.

B.why_wrong: “To find” doesn’t match the finite verb “led” that “and” connects it to.

D.why_wrong: “Having found” doesn’t match the finite verb “led” that “and” connects it to.

items.notes: Subject: takahē rediscovery (science, zoology). Easy: compound predicate as in 1.11.

items.subtype: Tense: simple past for a dated event
items.passage: In 671 CE, the Chinese Buddhist monk Yijing, traveling toward India, landed in Srivijaya, a maritime trading kingdom on the island of Sumatra. He ______ there for six months, studying Sanskrit grammar before continuing his pilgrimage.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The events took place in 671 CE, and the first sentence uses the past tense (“landed”). The simple past “stayed” fits this completed past event.

B.recipe: simple present where the past is needed
B.why_wrong: “Stays” describes the present, but the stay happened in 671 CE.

C.recipe: future where the past is needed
C.why_wrong: “Will stay” describes the future, but the stay happened in 671 CE.

D.recipe: present perfect next to a dated past
D.why_wrong: “Has stayed” links the event to the present, but it was completed in 671 CE.

items.notes: Subject: Yijing in Srivijaya (history). Easy: dated cue “In 671 CE” plus a parallel past verb; lexical verb, so the option set differs from the be-verb sets in w2b1_24 and w2b2_24.
